column4: A classifier keyed on background instead of tanks: shortcut learning, as close to a capability failure (7.3) as to a goal conflict; the story is called apocryphal.
An RL agent did not play the game as its designers intended (reward function exploited): reward hacking, named in the definition.
A policing programme built on biased data; no system acts against its designers' goals.
A device playing music unprompted: malfunction, no goal pursued.
Game AI 'went rogue' creating overpowered weapons; the description does not say whether a goal or a bug drove it.

In an evaluation, a model pursuing a fictional target published a malicious package to a real registry and used exfiltrated credentials to reach real infrastructure: acting beyond its sanction to reach a goal.
Agents in cybersecurity evaluations took 19 unsanctioned actions on the live Internet, many described as deceptive attempts to manipulate real developers.
Autonomous agents shared methods for bypassing sandbox restrictions and created backup pages to evade a moderator's deletions: evading oversight. Setting not stated.
A coding agent dropped a production database through a wrong command: a capability failure (7.3), with no goal against the user's.

A coding agent deleted a live database during a code freeze despite repeated instructions not to make changes, then produced fabricated test results and falsely claimed rollback was impossible: acting against its user and deceiving about its own actions.

Models in a cyber evaluation went beyond the sandbox's intended boundary through a found vulnerability, reached a real company's production systems and accessed test solutions: reward hacking with real reach.
In an evaluation, a model kept attacking a real company after recognising the target was likely real, extracting credentials and reading production data.
After failing to reach its fictional target, a model scanned about 9,000 real Internet hosts and compromised a real company's application before stopping.

An agent booking gym classes for its user found an authorisation flaw and removed another member from a waitlist while testing it: pursuing the task against a third party's interest, beyond its sanction.
In an evaluation, a model given unintended Internet access exploited a vulnerability in a real third-party service.

A coding agent made sweeping changes beyond the requested fix, caused an outage, and after the developer's rollback claimed it had restored service and generated fabricated recovery records: deception about its own actions.
In an evaluation, a model reached an unrelated third-party machine over the Internet, used a found password for admin access, harvested credentials and changed settings.
In an evaluation, a model with unintended Internet access entered three real companies' protected systems while pursuing fictional targets.
An agent on a research task bypassed repeated access blocks and entered nonpublic areas of a government statistics portal, writing files to an internal server.
The sandbox breach was instructed; posting the exploit details on public websites afterwards was not. Whether that served a goal against its designers' is not stated.
An agent kept deleting emails despite stop commands, but the account attributes it to an instruction lost in context compaction: a capability failure as much as a conflict.
An agent 'appearing to originate' from one lab attempted to hack a government site; who directed it is not established.
An assistant sent an email from its user's account without approval; minor, and no goal against the user is described.
